l225.strum2: G, D, Em and C: one bar each, in quarter notes.

l231.title: Strumming quarter notes
l231.objective: Strum down once per beat, evenly and in time.
l231.s1: "Strumming means playing every string of the chord in one motion."
l231.s2: The pick sweeps from the chord's lowest string down to the 1st, with a loose wrist.
l231.s4: "Don't squeeze the pick: a stiff pick makes a stiff sound."
l231.c1b: The motion comes from the wrist, not the elbow, and crosses every string of the chord. Play the example: E minor, one strum per beat.
l231.c2b: Every strum at the same strength. Soft and even beats loud and uneven.
l231.pulse: Keep the pulse: the click stops after 8 beats and you carry on.
l231.strum: Strum Em downward in quarter notes, four bars.

l232.title: Down and up in eighth notes
l232.objective: Strum nonstop down-up eighth notes at 60 bpm or faster.
l232.s1: "Now the pick works on the way back too."
l232.s2: Down on the beat, up between beats: two strums per beat.
l232.s3: On the upstroke you don't need every string: the 3 or 4 highest are enough.
l232.s4: "Your hand never stops: it swings down and up like a pendulum."
l232.c1b: Down on "1, 2, 3, 4" and up on every "and". Play the example: A minor in eighth notes.
l232.c2b: The upstroke sounds softer and brighter: that's how it should be.
l232.tap: First just the alternation: one tap per click, ↓ and ↑ in turn. On the guitar, the ↑ goes between clicks.
l232.strum: Strum Am in down-up eighth notes, four bars.

l233.title: The ballad pattern
l233.objective: Play the down, down-up, up-down-up pattern with your hand always moving.
l233.s1: "Listen to this strum. You'll find it in tons of songs."
l233.s2: Down, down-up, (miss) up, down-up. It goes: "1, 2 and, and 4 and".
l233.s3: Your hand keeps the eighth-note pendulum, but twice it swings past without touching. Listen slowly.
l233.s4: "The trick: never stop your hand. If it stops, the pattern falls apart."
l233.c1b: ↓ · ↓ ↑ · ↑ ↓ ↑. Where there's a dot, your hand still moves down but misses the strings. Play the example: G major.
l233.c2b: Swinging past without touching is what keeps time. At first, say the pattern out loud as you play.
l233.strum: Strum G with the ballad pattern, four bars.

l234.title: Changing in time
l234.objective: Change chords inside the ballad pattern without losing the pulse.
l234.s1: "The secret of a good change: let go of the chord a little early."
l234.s2: On the last strum of the bar (the "and" of 4), your fingers are already heading to the new chord.
l234.s3: That last strum rings with open strings. That's fine: everyone does it.
l234.s4: "Listen: C, A minor, C, A minor. Two fingers stay in the same place."
l234.c1b: Lift your fingers on the last upstroke and land on the new chord right on "1". Play the example.
l234.c2b: C and A minor share two fingers: 1 on the 2nd string and 2 on the 4th. Keep them down and move only finger 3.
l234.strum1: C and Am with the ballad pattern, one bar each.
l234.strum2: G and C with the ballad pattern, one bar each.

l235.title: A progression in time
l235.objective: Play a 4-chord progression with the ballad pattern at 60, 70 and 80 bpm.
l235.s1: "Listen: E minor, C, G, D. Four chords, a whole song."
l235.s2: One bar each, then back to the start.
l235.s3: If one change trips you up, practice just that change ten times and go back to the progression.
l235.s4: "Once you've got it at 60, raise the tempo. This is music now!"
l235.c1b: Em, C, G and D, one bar each, with the ballad pattern. Play the example and follow the chords.
l235.c2b: Find the change that's hardest for you and practice it on its own: two strums on one chord, two on the other.
l235.strum1: Em, C, G and D with the ballad pattern.
l235.strum2: G, D, Em and C with the ballad pattern.

l241.title: The fifth on the 6th string
l241.objective: Play a power chord rooted on the 6th string without the other strings ringing.
l241.s1: "Listen to this with crunch. It's the sound of rock: the power chord."
l241.s2: Just two notes: finger 1 on the 6th string, fret 3, and finger 3 on the 5th, fret 5. That's G5.
l241.s3: The other strings don't ring: finger 1 resting on them and your picking-hand palm mute them.
l241.s4: "Neither major nor minor: the fifth sounds huge with lots of gain. Here it is clean."
l241.c1b: Finger 1 on the 6th, fret 3 (the root, in orange); finger 3 on the 5th, fret 5. The number on the right is the fret where the diagram starts. Play the example.
l241.c2b: Strum short, only the 6th and 5th. The rest is muted by finger 1 resting on the high strings.
l241.tap: Tap the two notes of G5 on the fretboard.
l241.play: Play G5 four times, once per beat. The app listens for the low note.
l241.strum: Strum G5 in quarter notes, two bars.

l242.title: Moving the fifth
l242.objective: Move the power chord along the 6th string and know which chord it is on each fret.
l242.s1: "The power chord shape is movable: the same on any fret."
l242.s2: The note on the 6th string gives the name: fret 3 = G, 5 = A, 8 = C, 10 = D.
l242.s3: Slide your hand without changing your finger shape.
l242.s4: "Four fifths and you've got a riff. Listen."
l242.c1b: The same shape on frets 3, 5, 8 and 10 of the 6th string. Play the example.
l242.c2b: Fret 3: G. 5: A. 7: B. 8: C. 10: D. 12: E, an octave above the open string.
l242.q1: On which fret of the 6th string is A5?
l242.play: Play G5, A5, C5 and D5, two beats each. The app listens for the low note.

l243.title: Root on the 5th string
l243.objective: Play power chords rooted on the 5th string.
l243.s1: "The same shape works one string over too."
l243.s2: Finger 1 on the 5th, fret 3, and finger 3 on the 4th, fret 5: C5.
l243.s3: Now the 6th string isn't played: mute it with the tip of finger 1.
l243.s4: "C, D, E and D: hear it climb and come back."
l243.c1b: Finger 1 on the 5th, fret 3 (root in orange); finger 3 on the 4th, fret 5. Play the example.
l243.tap: Tap the two notes of C5 on the fretboard.
l243.play: Play C5, D5, E5 and D5 rooted on the 5th string, two beats each.

l244.title: From the 6th to the 5th
l244.objective: Jump between power chords on the 6th and 5th strings in time.
l244.s1: "Let's mix them: some fifths on the 6th string and some on the 5th."
l244.s2: The shape doesn't change: you just move your hand from one string to the other.
l244.s3: G5 on the 6th and C5 on the 5th are on the same fret: 3.
l244.s4: "Less movement, more time to get there."
l244.c1b: G5 on the 6th; C5 and D5 on the 5th; back to G5. Play the example.
l244.c2b: From G5 to C5 your hand doesn't slide: finger 1 drops from the 6th to the 5th string on fret 3.
l244.tab: Read the tab (the low note of each fifth) and play each note on the fretboard.
l244.play: Play G5, C5, D5 and G5, two beats each.

l245.title: Power-chord riff
l245.objective: Play an original power-chord riff at 60 bpm or faster.
l245.s1: "Listen to this riff. Three power chords and a groovy rhythm."
l245.s2: The strum in each bar: down, down, down-up, down.
l245.s3: The chords: G5, A5, C5 (on the 5th string) and G5.
l245.s4: "First the strum in time, then the fretting hand. And finally, with crunch!"
l245.c1b: G5, A5, C5 and G5, one bar each, with the strum ↓ · ↓ · ↓ ↑ ↓ ·. Play the example.
l245.c2b: First the picking rhythm; then the notes. The app listens for strums in one exercise and for the low note in the other.
l245.play: Play the whole riff. The app listens for the low note of each fifth.

l251.title: Where to rest your palm
l251.objective: Rest your palm on the bridge to play muted notes (palm muting).
l251.s1: "Listen: the notes sound short and heavy. That's palm muting."
l251.s2: The edge of your palm barely touches the strings, right on top of the bridge.
l251.s3: Closer to the neck, the note chokes completely; on the bridge, it's muted but still has pitch.
l251.c1b: 1: the edge of your palm resting right on the bridge. 2: the strings sound short, but you still hear the note.
l251.c2b: Eighth notes on the open 6th string, muted. Play the example.
l251.c3b: The same with the string ringing open. Hear the difference from the one before.
l251.ear: Listen. Is it open or palm-muted?
l251.play: With palm muting, play the open 6th string once per beat.

l252.title: Palm-muted eighth notes
l252.objective: Play even, in-time muted eighth notes with your palm still.
l252.s1: "This sound drives a lot of rock riffs: muted eighth notes."
l252.s2: Your palm stays still on the bridge; only your wrist moves.
l252.s3: All downstrokes, so they sound the same.
l252.s4: "If your palm moves, the sound changes. Keep it still."
l252.c1b: Sixteen eighth notes on the open 6th string, palm-muted. Play the example and make sure they all sound the same.
l252.c2b: Palm-muted parts are usually played all downstrokes: the hits come out more even and heavier.
l252.play: Palm-muted eighth notes on the 6th string, with the metronome.

l253.title: Muted and open
l253.objective: Alternate muted notes with open accent notes.
l253.s1: "Palm muting shines when an open note suddenly jumps out."
l253.s2: Six muted eighth notes and, on beat 4, an open note: lift your palm.
l253.s3: After the open note, your palm goes back to the bridge.
l253.s4: "Muted, muted… open! That contrast is the whole point."
l253.c1b: In each bar, six muted eighth notes on the 6th and one open note on another string. Play the example and follow the tab.
l253.c2b: For the open note, lift your palm just a little. You don't need to move it far.
l253.play: Play the exercise: palm-muted eighth notes and one open note per bar.

l254.title: Palm-muted fifths
l254.objective: Play power chords in palm-muted eighth notes.
l254.s1: "Fifths plus palm muting: the sound of heavy rock."
l254.s2: E5 is the open 6th string plus the 5th string at fret 2. Then G5 and A5.
l254.s3: Downstroke eighth notes, with your palm on the bridge.
l254.s4: "Hear how it pushes. It's a freight train!"
l254.c1b: Two bars of E5 and one each of G5 and A5, in palm-muted eighth notes. Play the example.
l254.c2b: First the strum in time; then the notes. The app listens for the low note of each fifth.
l254.strum: Strum E5, E5, G5 and A5 in palm-muted eighth notes.
l254.play: Play the palm-muted eighth notes. The app listens for the low note.

l255.title: Palm-muted riff
l255.objective: Play an original riff with palm muting and open notes at 60 bpm or faster.
l255.s1: "Listen to this crunchy riff. It mixes everything from this module."
l255.s2: Muted eighth notes on the open 6th string answered by open notes.
l255.s3: The open notes are on the 6th and 5th strings, frets 3 and 5.
l255.s4: "Slow and even first. The gain does the rest."
l255.c1b: In the first three bars, four muted eighth notes and two open notes; the last one ends on a long note. Play the example and follow the tab.
l255.c2b: Practice it clean so the app hears you well; once you've got it, turn up the gain and enjoy it.
l255.play: Play the whole riff with the metronome.

l261.title: The pentatonic box
l261.objective: Find the A minor pentatonic at fret 5 and know where the root is.
l261.s1: "This five-note scale is the favorite for rock and blues solos."
l261.s2: A minor pentatonic: two notes per string, between frets 5 and 8.
l261.s3: The root, A, is in orange: on the 6th and 1st strings at fret 5, and on the 4th at fret 7.
l261.s4: "Hear it climb. Sound like a guitar solo?"
l261.c1b: The drawing starts at fret 5. Finger 1 on fret 5, finger 3 on 7 and finger 4 on 8. The orange dots are the root, A.
l261.c2b: From the 6th to the 1st string, two notes per string. Play the example and follow the tab.
l261.q1: What is the root of this pentatonic?
l261.tap: Tap the first 6 notes of the box on the fretboard, from the 6th to the 4th string.

l262.title: Up and down
l262.objective: Play the pentatonic up and back in quarter notes at 60 bpm or faster.
l262.s1: "Now the whole box: up to the 1st string and back down to the 6th."
l262.s2: One finger per fret: 1 on fret 5, 3 on 7 and 4 on 8.
l262.s3: Alternate picking, even when you change strings.
l262.s4: "Once you know it by heart, watch the root: that's where solos start and end."
l262.c1b: Twelve notes up and twelve down. Play the example and follow the tab.
l262.c2b: On every string, finger 1 goes on fret 5. The other note is played by finger 3 (fret 7) or 4 (fret 8).
l262.play: Pentatonic up and back with the metronome.

l263.title: Pentatonic in eighth notes
l263.objective: Play the pentatonic in eighth notes with alternate picking.
l263.s1: "Same notes, twice as fast: eighth notes."
l263.s2: Two notes per beat, with alternate picking: down, up.
l263.s3: Each string lasts exactly one beat: the pick always starts a string with a downstroke.
l263.s4: "And at the end, a long root note. That's how a phrase ends."
l263.c1b: Up and down in eighth notes with A at the end. Play the example and follow the tab.
l263.c2b: With two notes per string, alternate picking makes every string start with a downstroke. Easy to remember.
l263.play: The pentatonic in eighth notes with the metronome.

l264.title: Your first phrase
l264.objective: Read and play a phrase built from the pentatonic.
l264.s1: "A solo isn't running the scale up and down: it's phrases."
l264.s2: This phrase moves down the box two notes at a time, climbs a little and rests on A.
l264.s3: It ends on the root, on the 4th string, fret 7. That makes it sound finished.
l264.s4: "Listen with crunch. It already sounds like a solo!"
l264.c1b: Four bars that move down the box, climb a little and end on A. Play the example and follow the tab.
l264.c2b: Phrases that end on the root sound closed. Try ending on another note and hear the difference.
l264.tab: Read the phrase in the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l264.play: Play the phrase with the metronome.

l265.title: Call and response
l265.objective: Answer one phrase with another using the pentatonic.
l265.s1: "Listen to this call: it rises and hangs in the air."
l265.s2: And this is the response: it comes down and returns to A.
l265.s3: Call and response together. That's how guitarists talk in a solo.
l265.s4: "Once you've got it, make up your own response with the notes of the box."
l265.c1b: Two bars that rise and end on E, a note that leaves things open. Play the example.
l265.c2b: Two bars that come down and end on A, the root. Play the example.
l265.play1: Play the response with the metronome.
l265.play2: Play the call and the response back to back.

cp3.intro: Show what you learned in level 3: legato, bends, vibrato, barre chords and the fretboard map.
cp3.legato: Play the legato phrase. The app waits for each note.
cp3.bend: Whole-step bend at fret 7 on the 3rd string, hold and release, twice.
cp3.vib: Fret 5 on the 1st string with vibrato for 4 seconds.
cp3.strum: F, G, Am and G barre chords in quarter notes at 70 bpm.
cp3.map: Tap the natural notes on the 5th string, from B to A.

l311.title: Hammer-on
l311.objective: Sound a second note by hammering a finger onto the string, without picking again.
l311.s1: "Can you play a note without the pick? Yes: hammer it with a finger."
l311.s2: Pick fret 5 on the 3rd string and, without picking again, hammer fret 7 with finger 3.
l311.s3: Listen: two notes, one pick stroke. It's called a hammer-on.
l311.s4: "The finger lands fast and firm, right behind the fret, like a hammer."
l311.c1b: 1: finger 1 presses fret 5 and you pick. 2: finger 3 slams onto fret 7 and the new note rings by itself.
l311.c2b: Fret 5 and fret 7 on the 3rd string, twice. In printed tabs it's marked with an "h" between the numbers.
l311.q1o1: Playing a note and sounding a higher one by hammering a finger, without picking
l311.q1o3: Muting the string with your palm
l311.play: Pick fret 5 and hammer on to fret 7 on the 3rd string, four times. The app waits for each note.

l312.title: Pull-off
l312.objective: Sound a lower note by plucking the string with your finger as you let go.
l312.s2: Finger 1 on fret 5 and finger 3 on fret 7. Pick, then pull finger 3 off, tugging the string a little.
l312.s3: Listen: fret 7 rings, then fret 5, with a single pick stroke.
l312.s4: "Don't lift the finger straight up: pull the string toward the floor, like a pinch."
l312.c1b: 1: finger 1 is already on fret 5. 2: finger 3 leaves, tugging the string down, and fret 5 rings.
l312.c2b: Fret 7 and fret 5 on the 3rd string, twice. In printed tabs it's marked with a "p".
l312.q1: In a pull-off, what does the leaving finger do?
l312.q1o1: Lifts straight up, without touching the string
l312.q1o2: Tugs the string a little as it lets go
l312.play: Pick fret 7 and pull off to fret 5 on the 3rd string, four times.

l313.title: Legato in the box
l313.objective: Climb the pentatonic with one pick stroke per string and a hammer-on for the second note.
l313.s1: "The pentatonic has two notes per string: perfect for legato."
l313.s2: Pick the first note on each string and hammer on the second.
l313.s3: It sounds smoother, as if the guitar were singing.
l313.c1b: From the 6th to the 1st string: pick fret 5 and hammer on to 7 or 8. Play the example and follow the tab.
l313.c2b: They're the same A pentatonic notes from level 2. Only the way you play them changes.
l313.play: Climb the pentatonic with hammer-ons. The app waits for each note.

l314.title: Hammer and pull together
l314.objective: Chain hammer-ons and pull-offs on the same string.
l314.s1: "Listen to this trill: up and down nonstop with one pick stroke."
l314.s2: Hammer from 5 to 7 and pull off from 7 to 5, again and again.
l314.s3: Finger 1 stays on fret 5 the whole time.
l314.s4: "Start slowly. Speed comes on its own."
l314.c1b: Frets 5 and 7 on the 3rd string in eighth notes, legato. Play the example and follow the tab.
l314.c2b: Finger 3 does all the work. Finger 1 stays firm on fret 5 so the pull-off has somewhere to land.
l314.play: Fret 5, hammer on to 7, pull off to 5: six times in a row, ending on 5.

l315.title: Legato phrase
l315.objective: Play a pentatonic phrase using hammer-ons and pull-offs.
l315.s1: "Listen to this crunchy phrase: you can barely hear the pick."
l315.s2: On each string: hammer on going up, pull off coming back.
l315.s3: It moves from the 1st to the 4th string and ends on A.
l315.s4: "Here it is slow and clean. Your turn."
l315.c1b: Four bars in the pentatonic box. Play the example and follow the tab.
l315.c2b: When two notes in a row are on the same string, the second is slurred: hammer-on going up, pull-off going down.
l315.tab: Read the phrase in the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l315.play: Play the phrase with legato. The app waits for each note.

l321.title: Slide up
l321.objective: Slide your finger from one fret to another without lifting it, landing right on the note.
l321.s1: "Hear how the note glides. That's a slide."
l321.s2: Play fret 7 on the 3rd string and slide up to 9 without lifting or easing off.
l321.s3: The target note rings by itself, with no extra pick stroke.
l321.s4: "Stop right on fret 9. Not before, not after."
l321.c1b: 1: the finger presses fret 7 and you pick. 2: it slides with the same pressure up to fret 9.
l321.c2b: From fret 7 to 9 on the 3rd string, twice. In printed tabs it's marked with "/".
l321.play: Slide from fret 7 to 9 on the 3rd string, three times. The app waits for each note.

l322.title: Slide down
l322.objective: Slide toward the headstock and land right on the note.
l322.s2: Fret 10 on the 2nd string, slide down to 8 with the same finger.
l322.s3: It's easier to overshoot going down: stop decisively.
l322.s4: "Listen when you arrive: the note has to be in tune."
l322.c1b: From fret 10 to 8 on the 2nd string, twice. In printed tabs it's marked with "\".
l322.c2b: Ease off on the way and the note dies before it arrives. Press too hard and it brakes. Find the middle.
l322.play: Slide from fret 10 to 8 on the 2nd string, three times.

l323.title: Sliding to a new position
l323.objective: Use a slide to move your hand to another area of the neck without breaking the phrase.
l323.s1: "The box isn't a cage: a slide gets you out."
l323.s2: Frets 5 and 7 on the 3rd string, slide to 9, then continue on the 2nd string, frets 8 and 10.
l323.s3: The slide is a bridge: your hand is already in the new area.
l323.s4: "Hear the phrase climb without a break."
l323.c1b: Five notes: 5 and 7, slide to 9 on the 3rd string, then 8 and 10 on the 2nd. Play the example and follow the tab.
l323.c2b: That's how you move from one pentatonic box to the next. In level 4 you'll learn all five.
l323.play: Play the five notes with the slide. The app waits for each note.

l324.title: Phrase with slides
l324.objective: Play a phrase that slides up and back on three strings.
l324.s1: "Listen: on each string, the phrase slides up and comes back down."
l324.s2: Frets 8 and 10 on the 1st and 2nd strings; 7 and 9 on the 3rd.
l324.s3: Slide going up; coming down, slide or pull off, whichever is cleaner for you.
l324.s4: "Like this, slow and clean. Now you!"
l324.c1b: Four bars moving from the 1st to the 4th string and ending on A. Play the example and follow the tab.
l324.c2b: Notice which notes are on the same string: the slide goes between them.
l324.tab: Read the phrase in the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l324.play: Play the phrase with slides. The app waits for each note.

l331.title: Your first bend
l331.objective: Bend the string a half step and land right on the note.
l331.s1: "Listen: the note rises like a voice. That's a bend."
l331.s2: You push the string with finger 3, helped by fingers 1 and 2, toward the 6th string.
l331.s3: First listen to the target note; then the bend that reaches it.
l331.s4: "A half step is small: a little nudge. The app tells you if you got there."
l331.c1b: 1: fingers 1 and 2 help behind finger 3. 2: push the string toward the 6th. 3: the note rises to the target.
l331.c2b: First fret 9 on the 2nd string (the target note), then the bend from fret 8 up to that same note.
l331.q1: On the 2nd string, which way do you push to bend?
l331.bend: Half-step bend at fret 8 on the 2nd string. Hold it when you get there. Three times.

l332.title: Whole-step bend
l332.objective: Bend the string a whole step and hold the note in tune.
l332.s1: "The whole-step bend is the most used in solos. Listen."
l332.s2: Fret 7 on the 3rd string: D. The bend takes it to E, the sound of fret 9.
l332.s3: It takes more strength: push with three fingers and rotate your wrist a little, like turning a doorknob.
l332.s4: "Fall short and it sounds out of tune. Better to land right on it."
l332.c1b: First fret 9 (the note you need to reach), then the bend from 7. Play the example.
l332.c2b: The strength doesn't come from the finger but from the rotating wrist. Your thumb can peek over the neck for leverage.
l332.bend: Whole-step bend at fret 7 on the 3rd string, four times.

l333.title: Hear it before you push
l333.objective: Keep the target note in your ear and tune the bend to it.
l333.s1: "The secret of an in-tune bend is in your ear, not your finger."
l333.s2: First play the target note (fret 9) and listen to it carefully.
l333.s3: Then bend from 7 and compare it with what's in your head.
l333.s4: "That's how guitarists practice: target, bend, target, bend."
l333.c1b: Fret 9, bend from 7, fret 9, bend from 7. Play the example and compare.
l333.c2b: If the bend sounds "low" next to the target, push a little more. If it sounds "high", you went too far.
l333.play: On the 3rd string: fret 9, fret 7, then fret 9 again, the target note.
l333.bend: Now bend from fret 7 up to that note, three times.

l334.title: Bend and release
l334.objective: Bend up, hold and return to the starting note without it dying.
l334.s1: "Listen: up, it holds, and back down. Bend and release."
l334.s2: Bend, hold the note and slowly let the string back to the starting note.
l334.s3: Don't lift your fingers: the note keeps ringing as it comes down.
l334.s4: "Coming down under control matters as much as going up."
l334.c1b: Whole-step bend at fret 7 on the 3rd string and back, twice. Play the example.
l334.c2b: If the note dies on the way down, keep finger 3's pressure while the string goes back into place.
l334.bend: Whole-step bend at fret 7 on the 3rd string, hold and release, three times.

l335.title: Bends in a phrase
l335.objective: Play whole-step bends on the 2nd and 3rd strings inside a phrase.
l335.s1: "Hear how a bend makes the phrase talk."
l335.s2: Fret 8 on the 2nd string: G. A whole-step bend takes it to A, the root.
l335.s3: The phrase ends on A, with vibrato. Vibrato is coming in the next module.
l335.s4: "A bend that lands on the root sounds like the end of a solo."
l335.c1b: Two notes on the 1st string, a whole-step bend on the 2nd and an ending on A with vibrato. Play the example and follow the tab: the arrow marks the bend.
l335.c2b: Fret 8 on the 2nd string (G → A) and fret 7 on the 3rd (D → E): both are in the pentatonic box.
l335.bend1: Whole-step bend at fret 8 on the 2nd string, three times.
l335.bend2: Whole-step bend at fret 7 on the 3rd string, three times.

l341.title: Wrist vibrato
l341.objective: Make the note waver with small repeated bends driven from the wrist.
l341.s1: "Listen: the note shimmers, like a singing voice. That's vibrato."
l341.s2: It's tiny bends, up and back, one after another.
l341.s3: Compare: the same note without vibrato…
l341.c1b: 1: the finger presses firmly. 2: the wrist rotates a little and back, several times a second; the note barely rises and falls.
l341.c2b: Fret 10 on the 2nd string with vibrato. Play the example.
l341.vib: Fret 10 on the 2nd string with vibrato for 4 seconds.

l342.title: Even vibrato
l342.objective: Keep a vibrato even in speed and width for 6 seconds.
l342.s1: "A good vibrato is even: same speed, same width."
l342.s2: Count in your head: about five waves per second.
l342.s3: If it speeds up or slows down, the app will tell you.
l342.s4: "Even first. Then add your own style."
l342.c1b: Fret 5 on the 1st string (A) with a steady vibrato. Play the example.
l342.c2b: Not too slow (it sounds out of tune) or too fast (it sounds nervous). Between 4 and 7 waves per second works well.
l342.vib: Fret 5 on the 1st string with an even vibrato for 6 seconds.

l343.title: Wide vibrato
l343.objective: Make a wider vibrato, for long notes with gain.
l343.s1: "With crunch, a wide vibrato sounds huge. Listen."
l343.s2: Each wave is like a slightly bigger bend.
l343.s3: Fret 7 on the 4th string: A. Push with help from the other fingers.
l343.s4: "Wider doesn't mean faster: keep the speed."
l343.c1b: Fret 7 on the 4th string with a wide vibrato and crunch. Play the example.
l343.c2b: Just like a bend, fingers 1 and 2 help behind finger 3. The wrist does the work.
l343.vib: Fret 7 on the 4th string with a wide vibrato for 5 seconds.

l344.title: Ending with vibrato
l344.objective: Play a phrase and close it with a long note with vibrato.
l344.s1: "Listen: four notes and a long note that shimmers. That's how solo phrases end."
l344.s2: The first notes, short and precise.
l344.s3: The last one, long: as soon as it rings, start the vibrato.
l344.s4: "Your vibrato is your signature. Every guitarist has their own."
l344.c1b: Four quarter notes and A on the 4th string with vibrato. Play the example and follow the tab: the wave marks the vibrato.
l344.c2b: On long notes and at the end of phrases. On fast notes there's no time, and no need.
l344.play: Play the five notes of the phrase. The app waits for each note.
l344.vib: Now the final note, A at fret 7 on the 4th string, with vibrato for 4 seconds.

l351.title: Finger 1 lying flat
l351.objective: Make all 6 strings ring with finger 1 lying across one fret (a barre).
l351.s1: "A barre turns your finger 1 into a movable nut."
l351.s2: Lay finger 1 across all 6 strings at fret 5, using its side, not the pad.
l351.s3: Listen: all six strings have to ring clean.
l351.s4: "If one buzzes, roll your finger slightly or move it closer to the fret."
l351.c1b: In the diagram, the gold bar is finger 1 lying flat. Practice just the barre first, no other fingers, at fret 5.
l351.c2b: Your thumb goes behind the neck, behind finger 1. Pull your arm back a little: its weight does half the work.
l351.q1: Which part of finger 1 makes the barre?
l351.play: With a barre at fret 5, play the 6 strings one at a time. The app waits for each note.

l352.title: F major (F)
l352.objective: Play the F barre chord with every note clean and strum it in time.
l352.s2: It's the E major shape with a barre at fret 1.
l352.s3: First the notes one at a time: if one doesn't ring, shift finger 1 slightly until it does.
l352.s4: "And with the ballad pattern. Now you have a chord that moves all over the neck!"
l352.c1b: Diagram: finger 1 lying across all 6 strings at fret 1; finger 2 on the 3rd, fret 2; fingers 3 and 4 on the 5th and 4th, fret 3. The gold bar is the barre. Play the example: the notes one at a time.
l352.c2b: It's the guitar's most feared chord. The trick isn't squeezing harder: use the bony side of finger 1, not the pad, and pull your elbow back a little.
l352.tap: Tap the notes your fingers press in F on the fretboard (the barre stays underneath).
l352.arp: Hold F and play its strings one at a time, low to high. The app waits for each note.
l352.strum: Strum F downward, once per beat.

l353.title: F minor (Fm)
l353.objective: Play the Fm barre chord with every note clean and strum it in time.
l353.s2: It's the E minor shape with a barre at fret 1.
l353.s3: First the notes one at a time: if one doesn't ring, shift finger 1 slightly until it does.
l353.s4: "And with the ballad pattern. Now you have a chord that moves all over the neck!"
l353.c1b: Diagram: finger 1 lying across fret 1; fingers 3 and 4 on the 5th and 4th, fret 3. The 3rd string rings from the barre. The gold bar is the barre. Play the example: the notes one at a time.
l353.c2b: It's F major without finger 2: the barre alone has to make the 3rd string ring. Check that string in the arpeggio.
l353.tap: Tap the notes your fingers press in Fm on the fretboard (the barre stays underneath).
l353.arp: Hold Fm and play its strings one at a time, low to high. The app waits for each note.
l353.strum: Strum Fm downward, once per beat.

l354.title: Moving the barre
l354.objective: Move the E-shape barre chord along the neck and know which chord it is on each fret.
l354.s1: "The F shape can move to any fret."
l354.s2: At fret 3 it's G; at fret 5, A. Like power chords: the 6th string gives the name.
l354.s3: The E minor shape works the same: at fret 5 it's A minor (Am).
l354.c1b: The F shape at fret 3. Play the example.
l354.c2b: The F minor shape at fret 5. Play the example.
l354.q1: The E major barre shape at fret 5: which chord is it?
l354.arp: Hold the G barre chord at fret 3 and play its strings one at a time.
l354.strum: G and Am barre chords, two bars each, in half notes.

l355.title: Barre chord progression
l355.objective: Play a barre chord progression in time.
l355.s1: "Listen: F, G, A minor and G, all with barres."
l355.s2: Between F and G the shape stays the same: it just moves two frets.
l355.s3: From G to A minor, the shape changes from major to minor and moves up two frets.
l355.s4: "Once you've got it in quarter notes, switch to the ballad pattern."
l355.c1b: F, G, Am and G, one bar each. Play the example.
l355.c2b: To move, relax the barre without lifting it and slide it. Squeeze again only at the new fret.
l355.strum1: F, G, Am and G in quarter notes.
l355.strum2: F, G, Am and G with the ballad pattern.

l361.title: B flat major (Bb)
l361.objective: Play the Bb barre chord with every note clean and strum it in time.
l361.s2: It's the A major shape with a barre at fret 1.
l361.s3: First the notes one at a time: if one doesn't ring, shift finger 1 slightly until it does.
l361.s4: "And with the ballad pattern. Now you have a chord that moves all over the neck!"
l361.c1b: Diagram: finger 1 lying across fret 1 from the 5th string; fingers 2, 3 and 4 on the 4th, 3rd and 2nd, fret 3. Don't play the 6th. The gold bar is the barre. Play the example: the notes one at a time.
l361.c2b: Three fingers on fret 3 leave little room: if it's hard, many guitarists lay finger 3 flat across those three strings.
l361.tap: Tap the notes your fingers press in Bb on the fretboard (the barre stays underneath).
l361.arp: Hold Bb and play its strings one at a time, low to high. The app waits for each note.
l361.strum: Strum Bb downward, once per beat.

l362.title: C major with a barre (C)
l362.objective: Play the C barre chord with every note clean and strum it in time.
l362.s1: "Listen: this is C major with a barre."
l362.s2: It's the A major shape with a barre at fret 3.
l362.s3: First the notes one at a time: if one doesn't ring, shift finger 1 slightly until it does.
l362.s4: "And with the ballad pattern. Now you have a chord that moves all over the neck!"
l362.c1b: Diagram: finger 1 lying across fret 3 from the 5th string; fingers 2, 3 and 4 on the 4th, 3rd and 2nd, fret 5. Don't play the 6th. The gold bar is the barre. Play the example: the notes one at a time.
l362.c2b: It's the B flat shape two frets higher. It sounds brighter than the open C.
l362.tap: Tap the notes your fingers press in C on the fretboard (the barre stays underneath).
l362.arp: Hold C and play its strings one at a time, low to high. The app waits for each note.
l362.strum: Strum C downward, once per beat.

l363.title: C minor (Cm)
l363.objective: Play the Cm barre chord with every note clean and strum it in time.
l363.s2: It's the A minor shape with a barre at fret 3.
l363.s3: First the notes one at a time: if one doesn't ring, shift finger 1 slightly until it does.
l363.s4: "And with the ballad pattern. Now you have a chord that moves all over the neck!"
l363.c1b: Diagram: finger 1 lying across fret 3 from the 5th string; finger 3 on the 4th and finger 4 on the 3rd, fret 5; finger 2 on the 2nd, fret 4. Don't play the 6th. The gold bar is the barre. Play the example: the notes one at a time.
l363.c2b: Compared with C major, only one note changes: the one on the 2nd string drops a fret.
l363.tap: Tap the notes your fingers press in Cm on the fretboard (the barre stays underneath).
l363.arp: Hold Cm and play its strings one at a time, low to high. The app waits for each note.
l363.strum: Strum Cm downward, once per beat.

l364.title: D minor with a barre (Dm)
l364.objective: Play the Dm barre chord with every note clean and strum it in time.
l364.s1: "Listen: this is D minor with a barre."
l364.s2: It's the A minor shape with a barre at fret 5.
l364.s3: First the notes one at a time: if one doesn't ring, shift finger 1 slightly until it does.
l364.s4: "And with the ballad pattern. Now you have a chord that moves all over the neck!"
l364.c1b: Diagram: finger 1 lying across fret 5 from the 5th string; fingers 3 and 4 on the 4th and 3rd, fret 7; finger 2 on the 2nd, fret 6. Don't play the 6th. The gold bar is the barre. Play the example: the notes one at a time.
l364.c2b: It's the C minor shape two frets higher: barre shapes move as a whole.
l364.tap: Tap the notes your fingers press in Dm on the fretboard (the barre stays underneath).
l364.arp: Hold Dm and play its strings one at a time, low to high. The app waits for each note.
l364.strum: Strum Dm downward, once per beat.

l365.title: E and A shapes together
l365.objective: Combine barre chords of both shapes without moving your hand much.
l365.s1: "Listen: A minor, D minor, G, C. All barre chords, all close together."
l365.s2: A minor and G use the E shape (6th string); D minor and C use the A shape (5th string).
l365.s3: A minor and D minor are on the same fret: 5. G and C, on 3.
l365.s4: "With two shapes you can find any chord within a few frets."
l365.c1b: Am, Dm, G and C, one bar each. Play the example.
l365.c2b: From Am to Dm the barre stays on the same fret: only the shape changes from the 6th to the 5th string.
l365.strum1: Am, Dm, G and C in quarter notes.
l365.strum2: Am, Dm, G and C with the ballad pattern.

l371.title: Notes on the 6th string
l371.objective: Find every natural note on the 6th string up to fret 12.
l371.s1: "To move chords and scales around you need to know where each note is."
l371.s2: Natural notes are the ones without sharps: E, F, G, A, B, C and D.
l371.s3: Between E and F, and between B and C, there's one fret. Between the rest, two.
l371.s4: "At fret 12 you find E again, an octave higher."
l371.c1b: Open E; fret 1 F; 3 G; 5 A; 7 B; 8 C; 10 D; 12 E.
l371.c2b: The natural notes on the 6th string, from open to fret 12. Play the example and follow the tab.
l371.q1: Which note is at fret 5 on the 6th string?
l371.tap: Tap the natural notes on the 6th string: F, G, A, B, C, D and E.

l372.title: Notes on the 5th string
l372.objective: Find every natural note on the 5th string up to fret 12.
l372.s1: "Now the 5th: that's where the roots of the A shape live."
l372.s2: It starts on A. Then B at 2, C at 3, D at 5.
l372.s3: E at 7, F at 8, G at 10 and A again at 12.
l372.s4: "With the 6th and 5th strings you can place any power chord or barre."
l372.c1b: Open A; fret 2 B; 3 C; 5 D; 7 E; 8 F; 10 G; 12 A.
l372.c2b: The natural notes on the 5th string, from open to fret 12. Play the example and follow the tab.
l372.q1: Which note is at fret 3 on the 5th string?
l372.tap: Tap the natural notes on the 5th string: B, C, D, E, F, G and A.

l373.title: The octave trick
l373.objective: Find the same note an octave higher: two strings up and two frets along.
l373.s1: "Not sure which note it is? Find its octave."
l373.s2: From the 6th string: the same note is on the 4th, two frets further along.
l373.s3: G at fret 3 on the 6th; G at fret 5 on the 4th. Listen.
l373.s4: "With this trick, if you know the 6th string, you know the 4th."
l373.c1b: Finger 1 on the 6th string and finger 3 on the 4th, two frets along. Both notes are the same, an octave apart. Play the example.
l373.c2b: To find notes fast and to play fat melodies: both notes together, muting the 5th string.
l373.tap: Tap G, A and C on the 6th string and their octaves on the 4th.
l373.play: Play each note and its octave: G, A and C. The app waits for each note.

l374.title: Find the chord
l374.objective: Use the 6th- and 5th-string maps to place any barre chord.
l374.s1: "Let's put it all together: where is C with a barre?"
l374.s2: E shape: find C on the 6th string, fret 8.
l374.s3: A shape: find C on the 5th string, fret 3. Two places for the same chord.
l374.s4: "Listen: G and C barre chords, both at fret 3."
l374.c1b: For the E shape (and power chords on the 6th).
l374.c2b: For the A shape (and power chords on the 5th).
l374.q1: C with the E shape: which fret is the barre on?
l374.q2: D with the A shape: which fret is the barre on?
l374.tap: Tap G on the 6th string and G on the 5th string.

cp4.intro: Final project: the neck map, fast picking, effects, the eight-bar solo and your own improvisation.
cp4.map: Tap box 3 of the A pentatonic on the fretboard, low to high.
cp4.fast: The sequence in groups of four, in eighth notes at 90 bpm.
cp4.chain: What is the usual order of the chain?
cp4.improv: Improvise three passes over the track, landing on a chord tone at each change.

l4101.title: Key and progression
l4101.objective: Pick the track, recognize its key and the scale to improvise with.
l4101.s1: "Final project: your own solo, with your sound, over a track."
l4101.s2: The track: Am – G – F – G. It's in A minor.
l4101.s3: "Use what you already know: the A pentatonic in any of its boxes."
l4101.s4: There's also a bluesier track: Am – Dm – Am – Em.
l4101.c1b: Am – G – F – G at 80 bpm. Listen several times and sing over it.
l4101.c2b: Am – Dm – Am – Em: the same scale works.
l4101.q1: To improvise over Am – G – F – G, which scale do you use?

l4102.title: Write your phrases
l4102.objective: Write the first half of the solo with a motif and target notes.
l4102.s1: Listen to the start of the model solo.
l4102.s2: "A good solo is built a few phrases at a time."
l4102.s3: Bar 1: the motif. Bar 2: a long note with vibrato.
l4102.s4: Bar 3: the motif again, ending on A. Bar 4: a long note.
l4102.c1b: Four bars: motif, long note, motif, long note. Play it as is or change it to taste.
l4102.c2b: Change notes in the motif, but keep the rhythm and land on a chord tone in each bar.
l4102.play: Play the first half of the model solo in time.
l4102.improv: Now improvise your own first half, landing on a chord tone at each change.

l4103.title: Putting the solo together
l4103.objective: Play an eight-bar solo with a beginning, a climb and an ending.
l4103.s1: Listen to the full solo, with distortion and delay.
l4103.s2: Bars 1 to 4 in box 1; bars 5 to 7 climb to box 2 and come back down.
l4103.s3: The ending: a long A with wide vibrato.
l4103.s4: "A solo tells a story: it starts calm, builds and closes."
l4103.c1b: Eight bars over two passes of the track. Notes marked ~ get vibrato.
l4103.c2b: This is how it sounds with distortion and delay. For the app, play it clean or with crunch.
l4103.play: Play the full solo in time.

l4104.title: Your solo over the track
l4104.objective: Improvise three passes in a row over the track with everything you've learned.
l4104.s1: Listen to the model solo with reverb, over the track.
l4104.s2: "Now it's yours: three passes, no safety net."
l4104.s3: Motifs, rests, target notes, box changes, bends and vibrato.
l4104.s4: "Record yourself on your phone and listen back. That's how you improve."
l4104.c1b: Three passes of Am – G – F – G.
l4104.c2b: Tune up, choose your sound and breathe. Think about where you'll end.
l4104.improv: Improvise three passes over the track. Land on a chord tone at each change.

l411.title: The pentatonic has five boxes
l411.objective: Review box 1 from memory, find its roots and learn that five boxes cover the neck.
l411.s1: "The box you know is just one of five. Together they cover the whole neck."
l411.s2: Box 1 of A minor at fret 5: two notes per string, with the roots (A) in red.
l411.s3: Each box starts where the previous one ends: the top note of one is the bottom note of the next.
l411.s4: Listen to all of box 1, from the 6th string to the 1st.
l411.c1b: Finger 1 on fret 5 and finger 3 or 4 two or three frets higher. The roots (A) are on the 6th, 4th and 1st strings.
l411.c2b: Twelve notes, from lowest to highest. Play it without looking until you know it by heart.
l411.q1: How many boxes does the pentatonic have?
l411.q2: Which note is the root of the A minor pentatonic?
l411.play: Box 1 up and back, without looking at the tab. The app waits for each note.

l412.title: Box 2
l412.objective: Play the second box of the A minor pentatonic, between frets 7 and 10.
l412.s1: "One step up: box 2 starts where box 1 had finger 4."
l412.s2: Your hand sits between frets 7 and 10: finger 1 on 7 and finger 4 on 10.
l412.s3: Listen to all of box 2. The same five notes, in another spot on the neck.
l412.s4: "Find the roots: in this box, A is on the 4th string (fret 7) and the 2nd (fret 10)."
l412.c1b: The bottom notes of this box are the top notes of box 1. That's why the boxes link up.
l412.c2b: From the 6th string to the 1st, two notes per string.
l412.tap: Tap box 2 on the fretboard, from lowest note to highest.
l412.play: Box 2 up and back on your guitar. The app waits for each note.

l413.title: Box 3
l413.objective: Play the third box, between frets 9 and 13, with the stretch on the 2nd string.
l413.s1: "Box 3 has a catch: on the 2nd string, finger 4 stretches to fret 13."
l413.s2: Finger 1 on fret 9 of the 3rd string; on the others, the box starts at 10 with finger 2.
l413.s3: Listen to box 3. The roots are on the 5th string (fret 12) and the 2nd (fret 10).
l413.s4: "If the stretch is hard, shift your hand a little instead of forcing the finger."
l413.c1b: It spans five frets: on the 3rd string it drops to 9 and on the 2nd it reaches 13.
l413.c2b: Twelve notes, low to high. Listen before you play it.
l413.tap: Tap box 3 on the fretboard, low to high.
l413.play: Box 3 up and back. Watch fret 13 on the 2nd string.

l414.title: Box 4
l414.objective: Play the fourth box, between frets 12 and 15.
l414.s1: "At fret 12 the guitar starts over: the notes match the open strings, an octave higher."
l414.s2: Finger 1 on fret 12 and finger 4 on 15; on the 4th and 3rd strings, finger 3 on 14.
l414.s3: Listen to box 4. The roots: 5th string at fret 12 and 3rd string at 14.
l414.s4: "Up here the frets are narrower: your fingers sit closer together."
l414.c1b: Almost the same on every string: frets 12 and 15, except the 4th and 3rd (12 and 14) and the 2nd (13 and 15).
l414.c2b: Low to high, two notes per string.
l414.tap: Tap box 4 on the fretboard, low to high.
l414.play: Box 4 up and back on your guitar.

l415.title: Box 5 and the full cycle
l415.objective: Play the fifth box (frets 2 to 5) and see that box 1 comes back after box 5.
l415.s1: "Box 5 sits right below box 1, near the nut."
l415.s2: Finger 1 on fret 2 and finger 4 on 5.
l415.s3: Its top note on each string is the bottom note of box 1: the cycle closes.
l415.c1b: Frets 3 and 5 on the 6th, 5th, 2nd and 1st strings; frets 2 and 5 on the 4th and 3rd.
l415.c2b: The same five notes as always: A, C, D, E and G.
l415.q1: If you keep climbing past box 4, which box comes next?
l415.q1o1: Box 5, the same one as on frets 2 to 5, twelve frets higher
l415.q1o3: None: the scale ends at fret 15
l415.tap: Tap box 5 on the fretboard, low to high.
l415.play: Box 5 up and back on your guitar.

l421.title: From box 1 to box 2
l421.objective: Move from box 1 to box 2 mid-phrase, with a slide.
l421.s1: "Boxes aren't cages: you can leave one and enter another without stopping."
l421.s2: Play box 1 up to the 3rd string. At fret 7 on that string, slide finger 3 up to 9.
l421.s3: Now you're in box 2: continue on the 2nd and 1st strings at frets 8 and 10.
l421.s4: Listen to the whole run, from box 1 to box 2.
l421.c1b: The 7-to-9 slide on the 3rd string moves your hand two frets up. From there your hand is in box 2, with finger 1 over fret 7.
l421.c2b: Twelve notes and a long one at the end, in box 2.
l421.play: Play the run: box 1, slide from 7 to 9 on the 3rd string, and box 2 to the top. The app waits for each note.

l422.title: Boxes 2, 3 and 4
l422.objective: Climb the 1st string from box 2 to box 4 and come back through box 3.
l422.s2: Start in box 2, on the 3rd string. When you reach the 1st, keep climbing on that string: frets 12 and 15.
l422.s3: Come down through box 3: fret 12 on the 1st, 13 and 10 on the 2nd, 12 and 9 on the 3rd.
l422.s4: "A single string works as a ladder between boxes."
l422.c1b: The way down goes through box 3. Watch the stretch on the 2nd string (fret 13).
l422.c2b: Up through boxes 2 and 4, down through 3.
l422.play: Play the run from box 2 to 4 and back through 3. The app waits for each note.

l423.title: Horizontal: one string
l423.objective: Play the pentatonic along the 1st string, from fret 5 to 17.
l423.s1: "Solos don't just go up and down: they also travel along the neck."
l423.s2: On the 1st string, the A pentatonic is at frets 5, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 17.
l423.s3: Listen: the same notes as in the boxes, but on one string.
l423.s4: "Use slides to move: the finger travels without leaving the string."
l423.c1b: Frets 5, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 17, and back. A very common shape for phrases that cross boxes.
l423.c2b: First play with one finger and slides. Then try fingers 1 and 3.
l423.tap: Tap the pentatonic on the 1st string, from fret 5 to 17.
l423.play: Up and down the 1st string: 5, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17 and back.

l424.title: On the diagonal
l424.objective: Cross the neck diagonally: from box 1 on the low strings to box 4 on the high ones.
l424.s1: "A diagonal run covers two octaves without trapping you in one box."
l424.s2: Start in box 1 (fret 5) on the 6th and 5th strings.
l424.s3: On the 4th string you move to box 2, on the 3rd to box 3, and on the two high strings you reach boxes 4 and 5.
l424.s4: "Two notes per string and a small hand jump at each change."
l424.c1b: Twelve notes climbing two octaves, from A to A.
l424.c2b: Slide your hand on the notes you play with finger 1: each new string drops you into the next box.
l424.tap: Tap the diagonal run on the fretboard, low to high.
l424.play: Play the diagonal: from box 1 on the 6th string up to fret 17 on the 1st.

l425.title: Other keys
l425.objective: Move the boxes to play the minor pentatonic in any key.
l425.s1: "What if the song is in E minor? The whole map moves."
l425.s2: Box 1 starts on the root on the 6th string. E is at fret 12 (or open).
l425.s3: Listen to box 1 in E minor, at fret 12: same shape, another key.
l425.s4: "Find the root on the 6th string and put finger 1 there."
l425.c1b: The five boxes have the same shape in every key. Only the starting fret changes.
l425.c2b: Box 1 in E minor: frets 12 to 15.
l425.q1: Box 1 in A minor starts at fret 5. Which fret does E minor start at?
l425.play: Box 1 in E minor (fret 12) up and back.

l431.title: The major scale by intervals
l431.objective: Build the major scale with the formula of whole and half steps.
l431.s1: "C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C. Why does it sound like that? Because of the distance between notes."
l431.s2: A half step is one fret. A whole step is two frets.
l431.s3: The major scale always follows the same formula: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
l431.s4: Listen to C major on one string: you can see and hear the two-fret and one-fret jumps.
l431.c1b: C major on the 5th string: frets 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 15. The two half steps are between 7 and 8 and between 14 and 15.
l431.c2b: W W H W W W H. Starting on any fret, this formula gives you that note's major scale.
l431.q1: What is the major scale formula?
l431.q1o1: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half
l431.q1o2: Whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole
l431.q1o3: Whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, half
l431.tap: Tap C major on the 5th string, from fret 3 to 15.
l431.play: C major on the 5th string: 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 15.

l432.title: G major in position
l432.objective: Play the G major scale with the root on the 6th string, without moving your hand.
l432.s1: "On one string you understand it; in position you play it fast."
l432.s2: Hand in 2nd position: one finger per fret, from 2 to 5.
l432.s3: The root, G, is at fret 3 on the 6th string. An octave up, at fret 5 on the 4th.
l432.s4: Listen to the scale going down, from the high G.
l432.c1b: Finger 1 on fret 2, finger 4 on 5. Roots in red. Play one octave first, then the full position.
l432.c2b: Eight notes: G, A, B, C, D, E, F♯ and G.
l432.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l432.play: G major, one octave up and back.

l433.title: C major from the 5th string
l433.objective: Play the major scale with the root on the 5th string: the module's second position.
l433.s1: "With the root on the 5th string you get another shape of the same scale."
l433.s2: C is at fret 3 on the 5th string. The scale climbs through the 4th and 3rd.
l433.s3: Listen to a short melody with these notes. That's the major sound: bright and happy.
l433.s4: "With these two shapes you can play any major scale by moving them to the root's fret."
l433.c1b: Frets 3 and 5 on the 5th string; 2, 3 and 5 on the 4th; 2, 4 and 5 on the 3rd.
l433.c2b: Made only of C major notes. It ends on E, which sounds stable over C.
l433.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l433.play: C major from the 5th string, one octave up and back.

l434.title: The natural minor scale
l434.objective: Play A natural minor and see that it's the pentatonic plus two notes.
l434.s1: "The natural minor scale sounds sadder, more serious."
l434.s2: A natural minor in 5th position: root at fret 5 on the 6th string.
l434.s3: Listen to one octave: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A.
l434.s4: "Look: it's your A minor pentatonic with B and F added."
l434.c1b: The position spans frets 4 to 8. Roots in red.
l434.c2b: Frets 5, 7 and 8 on the 6th string; 5, 7 and 8 on the 5th; 5 and 7 on the 4th.
l434.q1: Which notes does A natural minor have that the pentatonic doesn't?
l434.play: A natural minor, one octave up and back.

l435.title: Relatives: major and minor
l435.objective: Understand that C major and A minor share the same notes, and tell them apart by ear.
l435.s2: …and now a minor one. They use the same seven notes, but each revolves around its own root.
l435.s3: C major and A minor are relatives: same notes, different center.
l435.s4: "To go from a major key to its relative minor, go down three frets from the root."
l435.c1b: The minor shape with the root on the 5th string: D at fret 5. It's the relative minor of F major.
l435.c2b: Three frets below the major root is the root of its relative minor: from C (fret 8 on the 6th) to A (fret 5).
l435.q1: What is the relative minor of C major?
l435.ear1: Listen to the melody. Is it major or minor?
l435.ear2: And this one: major or minor?
l435.play: D minor from the 5th string, one octave up and back.

l441.title: What is a mode?
l441.objective: Understand that a mode is the major scale starting from another of its notes.
l441.s1: "Seven notes, seven starting points, seven different colors."
l441.s2: This is C major, from C to C.
l441.s3: Now the same notes, from D to D. It sounds minor, but different: it's the Dorian mode.
l441.s4: "No new scales to learn: change the center and you change the color."
l441.c1b: The notes of C major, starting and ending on D: D Dorian.
l441.c2b: Dorian (from the 2nd note), Phrygian (from the 3rd) and Mixolydian (from the 5th). The most used in rock, blues and funk.
l441.q1: If you play the notes of C major starting and ending on D, which mode is it?
l441.q2: How many modes come from the major scale?

l442.title: Dorian: minor with light
l442.objective: Play A Dorian and improvise with it over an Am and D track.
l442.s1: Listen to a Dorian lick over Am and D.
l442.s2: A Dorian is A minor with one note changed: F becomes F♯.
l442.s3: Hear it from A to A. That F♯ makes it less sad, ideal for funk, rock and blues.
l442.s4: "Over Am and D, F♯ sounds perfect because it's part of the D chord."
l442.c1b: Frets 5, 7 and 8 on the 6th string; 5, 7 and 9 on the 5th (fret 9 is the F♯); 5 and 7 on the 4th.
l442.c2b: A lick in A Dorian over Am – D. Notice when the F♯ shows up.
l442.play: A Dorian, one octave up and back.
l442.improv: Improvise in A Dorian over Am – D. Use the F♯ (fret 9 on the 5th string).

l443.title: Mixolydian: major with blues
l443.objective: Play A Mixolydian and improvise over A and G.
l443.s1: Listen to a Mixolydian lick over A and G.
l443.s2: A Mixolydian is A major with a lowered 7th: G instead of G♯.
l443.s3: Hear it from A to A: happy, but with a touch of rock and blues.
l443.s4: "Over A – G, it's the sound of hundreds of rock songs."
l443.c1b: Frets 5, 7 and 9 on the 6th string; 5, 7 and 9 on the 5th; 5 and 7 on the 4th.
l443.c2b: A lick in A Mixolydian over A – G.
l443.q1: Which note of A Mixolydian isn't in A major?
l443.play: A Mixolydian, one octave up and back.
l443.improv: Improvise in A Mixolydian over A – G.

l444.title: Phrygian: dark and tense
l444.objective: Play A Phrygian and improvise over Am and B♭.
l444.s1: Listen to a Phrygian lick over Am and B♭, with distortion.
l444.s2: A Phrygian is A minor with a lowered 2nd: B♭ instead of B.
l444.s3: Hear it from A to A. That half step between A and B♭ sounds dark: common in metal and flamenco.
l444.s4: "The B♭ chord over A is the Phrygian signature."
l444.c1b: Frets 5, 6 and 8 on the 6th string (6 is the B♭); 5, 7 and 8 on the 5th; 5 and 7 on the 4th.
l444.c2b: A lick in A Phrygian over Am – B♭.
l444.q1: What gives Phrygian its dark sound?
l444.q1o1: The minor 2nd: a half step between the root and the next note
l444.play: A Phrygian, one octave up and back.
l444.improv: Improvise in A Phrygian over Am – B♭.

l451.title: A motif and its variations
l451.objective: Repeat a short rhythmic idea and vary it, instead of running scales.
l451.s1: Listen: a three-note idea, repeated and changed in each bar.
l451.s2: "Improvising isn't running up the scale: it's saying something and repeating it with variations."
l451.s3: The motif: two eighth notes and a quarter note, then silence.
l451.s4: Over each chord, the same rhythm with other notes.
l451.c1b: Eighth, eighth, quarter and two beats of rest. Four bars, four variations.
l451.c2b: Am – G – F – G. The rhythm repeats and people remember it.
l451.play: Play the motif and its variations in time.

l452.title: Call and response
l452.objective: Build two-part phrases: one that stays open and one that closes.
l452.s1: Listen: one phrase rises and hangs in the air; the other falls and closes on A.
l452.s3: The question ends on E, which leaves the phrase open.
l452.s4: The answer ends on A, the root: it sounds like a full stop.
l452.c1b: It climbs the 3rd and 2nd strings, hits fret 5 on the 1st and stays on the E at fret 5 on the 2nd.
l452.c2b: It comes down box 1 and closes at fret 7 on the 4th string (A).

l453.title: Target notes
l453.objective: Land on a chord tone right when the chord changes.
l453.s1: Listen: at each chord change, the melody lands on a note of that chord.
l453.s2: "Every scale note works, but chord tones sound like a landing."
l453.s3: Over Am: A, C or E. Over G: G or D. Over F: A or C.
l453.s4: "Think about where you'll land, and land on beat 1."
l453.c1b: Each bar starts on a chord tone: A over Am, G over G, C over F and D over G.
l453.c2b: Hear how each bar starts on the right note.
l453.q1: Over the G chord, which A pentatonic note sounds like a landing note?
l453.play: Play the phrase with target notes in time.
l453.improv: Improvise over Am – G – F – G. At each change, land on a chord tone.

l454.title: Silence makes music too
l454.objective: Leave space in your phrases: play fewer notes and make each one count.
l454.s1: Listen: few notes, lots of air.
l454.s2: "A solo with rests breathes. One without rests wears you out."
l454.s3: Each phrase lasts one or two beats, then the track carries on alone.
l454.s4: "Let the last sound fade before you play the next."
l454.c1b: Five notes in four bars. The rhythm of the rests is part of the phrase.
l454.c2b: Count the rests out loud: "one, two, three, four."
l454.play: Play the phrase, respecting every rest.

l455.title: Your first improvisation
l455.objective: Improvise with box 1 over the track, using motifs, rests and target notes.
l455.s1: Listen to an example with everything from this module.
l455.s2: "It's time: the track plays and you decide what to play."
l455.s3: Use box 1, repeat a motif and leave rests.
l455.s4: "There are no wrong notes in the pentatonic: only choices."
l455.c1b: Am – G – F – G at 80 bpm. Listen until you feel the chord changes.
l455.c2b: Start with two or three notes. Repeat. Change one. Leave a rest. End on A.
l455.improv: Improvise with the A minor pentatonic over the track.

l461.title: Even eighth notes
l461.objective: Play eighth notes with alternate picking, even and in time, faster and faster.
l461.s1: "You don't chase speed: it comes when your picking is even and relaxed."
l461.s2: Down, up, down, up: always alternate, even when you change strings.
l461.s3: Listen to eighth notes at 70 bpm with the click.
l461.s4: "Small moves, from the wrist. The pick barely clears the string."
l461.c1b: Each eighth note switches direction. If your hand tenses up, lower the tempo.
l461.c2b: Frets 5 and 8 on the 1st and 2nd strings, in eighth notes.
l461.play: Even eighth notes at 70 bpm. Master them to unlock 85 and 100.

l462.title: String changes at speed
l462.objective: Run through box 1 in eighth notes without breaking the alternation.
l462.s1: "The problem isn't speed: it's changing strings without getting stuck."
l462.s2: Two notes per string: the pick always changes strings in the same direction.
l462.s3: Listen to box 1 in eighth notes at 60 bpm.
l462.s4: "Watch your picking hand for a few minutes: it should barely move."
l462.c1b: Box 1 goes up and down in eighth notes. It ends on the 6th string with an eighth rest.
l462.c2b: First at 60. Once it's clean, the app moves you up to 75 and 90.
l462.play: Box 1 in eighth notes, up and back, in time.

l463.title: Bursts
l463.objective: Play short fast groups and rest between them.
l463.s1: "A short, clean burst impresses more than a long, sloppy run."
l463.s2: Four fast eighth notes and a quarter note to breathe.
l463.s3: Listen to four bursts going down box 1.
l463.s4: "Relax your hand on each quarter note: that's your break."
l463.c1b: Four eighths, a quarter and a rest, four times. The last one ends with a half note on low A (fret 5, 6th string).
l463.c2b: Start at 80 bpm. Then 100 and 120 unlock.

l464.title: Groups of four
l464.objective: Play a sequence in four-note groups that climbs box 1.
l464.s1: "Sequences sound like real solos and train both hands."
l464.s2: Four notes from the box, and the next group starts one note higher.
l464.s3: Listen to the sequence at 70 bpm.
l464.c1b: Eight groups of four eighth notes, from the 6th string to the 1st.
l464.c2b: At 70 bpm first. Master it to unlock 90 and 110.
l464.play: Play the sequence in groups of four, in time.

l471.title: Double stops on strings 1 and 2
l471.objective: Play two strings at once with one finger, rock and roll style.
l471.s1: Listen: two notes together, with crunch.
l471.s2: One finger lying across the 1st and 2nd strings at fret 8.
l471.s3: "The pick hits only those two strings: the others stay silent."
l471.s4: Hear how it changes when you move to the 2nd and 3rd strings.
l471.c1b: Finger 3, slightly flattened, presses both strings. The pick makes a short stroke over the 2nd and 1st.
l471.c2b: First each note on its own to check they ring. Then together, in time.
l471.play: Play the two notes one at a time: fret 8 on the 2nd and fret 8 on the 1st, three times.
l471.strum: Now together, in quarter notes, with short downstrokes.

l472.title: Double stops on strings 2 and 3
l472.objective: Play double stops with two fingers and alternate them.
l472.s1: Listen: two double-stop positions that alternate.
l472.s2: Finger 1 at fret 7 on the 3rd string and finger 2 at fret 8 on the 2nd.
l472.s3: It alternates with the double stop from the previous lesson.
l472.s4: "Play only the two strings: mute the rest with your palm and spare fingers."
l472.c1b: Two fingers on neighboring frets. It's the basis of many blues and rock riffs.
l472.c2b: First one note at a time, then together in half notes.
l472.play: One at a time: fret 7 on the 3rd and fret 8 on the 2nd, three times.
l472.strum: Together, alternating with the double stop on strings 1 and 2, in half notes.

l473.title: Major triad on the high strings
l473.objective: Play the D major triad on the three high strings and arpeggiate it.
l473.s1: Listen to a three-note chord on the high strings.
l473.s2: A triad is three notes: root, 3rd and 5th. This is D major.
l473.s3: Hear it note by note: D, F♯ and A.
l473.s4: "Triads sound light: perfect for playing over another guitarist."
l473.c1b: Fret 7 on the 3rd string (finger 2), fret 7 on the 2nd (finger 3) and fret 5 on the 1st (finger 1). The shape moves to any root.
l473.tap: Tap the three notes of the D triad on the fretboard.

l474.title: Minor triad
l474.objective: Go from D major to D minor by changing just one note.
l474.s1: Listen to D major and then D minor.
l474.s2: Only the note on the 2nd string changes: from fret 7 to 6.
l474.s3: Listen to the D minor arpeggio: D, F and A.
l474.c1b: Fret 7 on the 3rd (finger 3), fret 6 on the 2nd (finger 2) and fret 5 on the 1st (finger 1).
l474.c2b: The same path as in major.
l474.q1: What changes between the major and minor triad?
l474.q1o1: The root goes up a half step
l474.q1o2: The 3rd goes down a half step
l474.q1o3: The 5th goes down a whole step

l475.title: Triads over the track
l475.objective: Arpeggiate the Am, G and F triads over the track, in time.
l475.s1: Listen: triad arpeggios following the track's chords.
l475.s2: "With triads, your guitar sketches the chords instead of playing them whole."
l475.s3: The three triads on the high strings: Am, G and F.
l475.s4: Am at frets 14-13-12, G at 12-12-10 and F at 10-10-8.
l475.c1b: One arpeggio per bar: Am, G, F and G.
l475.c2b: Hear how each arpeggio fits its chord.
l475.play: Arpeggiate the triads in time, one per bar.

l481.title: What is tapping?
l481.objective: Sound a note by hitting the string with a right-hand finger, then move to another with a pull-off.
l481.s1: Listen: fast notes far apart, with no pick.
l481.s2: A finger of your picking hand hits fret 12 on the 1st string, like a hammer-on.
l481.s3: That finger leaves with a pull-off and fret 5, held by finger 1, rings.
l481.s4: "Hold the pick between your thumb and finger 1, and tap with your middle finger."
l481.c1b: 1: the right-hand finger hits fret 12 and tugs the string as it lets go. 2: the other hand is already on frets 5 and 8.
l481.c2b: Fret 12 tapped and fret 5 with a pull-off, on the 1st string.
l481.q1o1: A finger of the picking hand, hitting the string
l481.q1o3: The palm resting on the bridge
l481.play: Tap fret 12 and pull off to 5 on the 1st string, four times. The app waits for each note.

l482.title: The 12-5-8 pattern
l482.objective: Play the classic three-note pattern: tap, pull-off and hammer-on.
l482.s1: Listen to the nonstop three-note pattern.
l482.s2: Tap at 12, pull off to 5 and hammer on to 8 with finger 4.
l482.s4: "All three notes should be equally loud. If 8 sounds weak, hammer harder."
l482.c1b: Three notes per tap: an A minor arpeggio with E, A and C.
l482.c2b: Slow and even. Mute the other strings with your left palm.
l482.play: 12-5-8 pattern on the 1st string, four times.

l483.title: Moving the tapping finger
l483.objective: Change the tapped note while the other hand stays put.
l483.s1: Listen: the tapped note climbs and the rest stays the same.
l483.s2: Twice at 12, twice at 13 and twice at 15. Frets 5 and 8 don't change.
l483.s3: "That's how you build a melody on top with an arpeggio below."
l483.c1b: Frets 12, 13 and 15 tapped; 5 and 8 with the left hand.
l483.c2b: Look at the fret before you tap. The finger lands right behind the fret, as when fretting.
l483.play: Play the pattern moving the tap: 12, 13, 15 and back to 12.

l484.title: Tapping on two strings
l484.objective: Move the tapping pattern from the 1st to the 2nd string.
l484.s2: On the 2nd string: tap at 15, pull off to 5 and hammer on to 8.
l484.s4: "When you change strings, both hands move together."
l484.c1b: Twice on the 1st string, twice on the 2nd and once on the 1st.
l484.c2b: Mute the string you just left with your right palm.
l484.play: Tapping pattern on the 1st, the 2nd and the 1st string again.

l491.title: Gain: overdrive and distortion
l491.objective: Tell clean, overdrive and distortion apart, and know how much gain each style needs.
l491.s1: Listen to the same lick clean…
l491.s2: …with overdrive: the sound gets a little dirty, like a pushed amp.
l491.s3: …and with distortion: more saturated, with more sustain. The sound of hard rock and metal.
l491.s4: "More gain isn't more sound: with too much, notes blur. Use just enough."
l491.c1b: 1: GAIN, how much saturation. 2: TONE, darker or brighter. 3: LEVEL, the volume with the pedal on.
l491.c2b: Lots of gain: it sustains long notes and bends. For chords, use less.
l491.play: Play the lick with your overdrive sound. The app waits for each note.

l492.title: Delay
l492.objective: Recognize delay and pick the repeat time to suit the style.
l492.s1: Listen: each note repeats behind it, quieter each time.
l492.s2: "Delay is an echo: it records what you play and plays it back a bit later."
l492.s3: A very short delay with a single repeat is called slapback: the rockabilly sound.
l492.s4: A long delay with several repeats makes a solo sound bigger.
l492.c1b: 1: TIME, how long each repeat takes. 2: FEEDBACK, how many repeats. 3: MIX, how loud they are.
l492.c2b: About 375 ms with three repeats: it fills the gaps between phrases.
l492.q1o1: A very short delay with one repeat
l492.q1o2: A long delay with many repeats
l492.play: Play the lick with a long delay. The app waits for each note.

l493.title: Reverb
l493.objective: Recognize reverb and know when to turn it down.
l493.s1: Listen to the lick with reverb: it sounds like a big hall.
l493.s2: "Reverb puts your guitar in a place: a room, a hall, a church."
l493.s3: Listen to the same lick without reverb: drier, closer.
l493.s4: "With lots of reverb, fast notes blend together. For riffs and rhythm, turn it down."
l493.c1b: An ambient tail that keeps ringing after each note.
l493.c2b: A little for rhythm and riffs; more for slow melodies and long notes.
l493.q1: When should you turn the reverb down?

l494.title: Modulation and wah
l494.objective: Recognize chorus and know what phaser and wah do.
l494.s1: Listen to some chords with chorus: the guitar sounds doubled and wavy.
l494.s2: "Chorus adds a slightly detuned copy that moves: like two guitars at once."
l494.s3: The same chords with no effect, to compare.
l494.s4: "A phaser makes a swirling sweep. A wah is a pedal you rock with your foot: high-low, like a voice saying 'wah'."
l494.c1b: Great for clean chords and arpeggios. With distortion, use it sparingly.
l494.c2b: The phaser swirls on its own, at the speed you choose. You move the wah with your foot, in time with what you play: big in funk.
l494.q1: What does a wah pedal do?
l494.q1o3: Sweeps from low to high as you move it with your foot

l495.title: The chain and your sound
l495.objective: Order the effects in the chain and set up one sound for rhythm and one for solos.
l495.s1: "Order matters: each pedal processes what it gets from the one before."
l495.s2: Guitar, tuner, wah, gain, modulation, delay, reverb and amp.
l495.s3: A rhythm sound: crunch, no delay, a little reverb.
l495.s4: A solo sound: more gain, delay and some reverb.
l495.c1b: 1: tuner. 2: wah. 3: overdrive or distortion. 4: chorus or phaser. 5: delay. 6: reverb. Same for pedals, a multi-effects unit or an app.
l495.c2b: Distortion, a delay of about 375 ms with two repeats, and low reverb.
l495.q1: Why does delay go after distortion?
l495.q1o1: So the already-distorted notes repeat and the echoes stay clean and clear
l495.q1o2: Because delay doesn't work with a clean signal
l495.q2: For a solo, what do you change from the rhythm sound?
l495.q2o1: Lower the gain and remove the delay
l495.q2o2: Raise the gain and add delay

checkpoint.2: Checkpoint 2 · Progression strummed and in p-i-m-a arpeggio
checkpoint.3: Checkpoint 3 · Barre chords, shuffle blues and a solo with slurs
checkpoint.4: Checkpoint 4 · II-V-I, bossa and improvising over the changes

goal.1_1: Know the parts of the classical guitar, its nylon strings, and tune it.
goal.1_2: Sit well and pluck with p-i-m-a and one finger per fret.
goal.1_3: Play free strokes and rest strokes, alternating i-m, with the thumb on the basses.
goal.1_4: Play the 1-2-3-4 chromatic cleanly on all 6 strings.
goal.1_5: Read tab with quarter notes, eighth notes and rests, including at sight.
goal.2_1: Play Em, Am, E, A and D cleanly, string by string.
goal.2_2: Add C, G, Dm, E7 and A7.
goal.2_3: Change chords in time without breaking the pulse.
goal.2_4: Strum in quarters and eighths, pop, ballad and with a slap.
goal.2_5: Accompany with arpeggios and alternating bass.
goal.2_6: Build the major scale and triads, and transpose with a capo.
goal.2_7: Play the minor pentatonic and improvise over Am.
goal.3_1: Play F and Bm with a half barre.
goal.3_2: Play F, Fm and F7 as barre chords and move them up the neck.
goal.3_3: Play B♭, Bm and Bm7 as barre chords and move them.
goal.3_4: Play a 12-bar blues with a shuffle feel.
goal.3_5: Slur notes up and down, and slide.
goal.3_6: Add the blue note and the major pentatonic.
goal.3_7: Strum zamba, chacarera, tango and waltz.
goal.4_1: Build the chords of a key and the II-V-I progression.
goal.4_2: Comp a II-V-I with 3-note shell chords.
goal.4_3: Play the bossa groove with an independent thumb.
goal.4_4: Connect the 5 pentatonic boxes across the neck.
goal.4_5: Play the major and natural minor scales in 2 positions.
goal.4_6: Improvise targeting chord tones on each change.
goal.5_1: Find any note and one chord in 5 places.
goal.5_2: Play triads on string sets and lead the voices.
goal.5_3: Play melody and chords together in an 8-bar arrangement.
goal.5_4: Use harmonics, pizzicato, tambora and i-m-a strumming.
goal.5_5: Improvise with Dorian, Mixolydian and Phrygian.
goal.5_6: Arrange and play a full song with the band.

l111.title: Meet your classical guitar
l111.objective: Name 9 parts of the classical guitar and identify the 6 strings by number and by sound.
l111.s1: "Hi! I'm Kordi. Today I'm playing a classical guitar: all wood, nylon strings and no cables."
l111.s2: Headstock, tuning pegs, nut, neck with frets, top, soundhole, bridge and saddle.
l111.s3: Six strings, from thickest to thinnest: E, A, D, G, B and E. Listen to them climb.
l111.s4: "There are two Es: the 6th, thick and low, and the 1st, thin and high. They are two octaves apart."
l111.c1t: The parts of the classical guitar
l111.c1b: Look at the drawing and find each number on your guitar. The body is hollow: the top vibrates and the soundhole lets the sound out. That's why it needs no amp.
l111.c2b: They are numbered from the thinnest: 1st E, 2nd B, 3rd G, 4th D, 5th A and 6th E. The 6th is on top, closest to your face.
l111.c3b: The thicker the string, the lower the sound. Listen to the 6th and the 1st: both are E, but two octaves apart.
l111.q2: What makes the classical guitar loud without an amp?
l111.q2o1: The body, with its top and soundhole
l111.ear: You'll hear both E strings. Which one is the high one?
l111.play: Play the open string that lights up, from the 6th to the 1st. Keep your phone near the soundhole.

l112.title: Nylon strings
l112.objective: Tell the wound bass strings from the plain nylon trebles, and know how to look after them.
l112.s1: "Did you notice my strings aren't all the same? The top ones shine like metal."
l112.s2: The three bass strings are wound: a nylon core wrapped in fine wire.
l112.s3: Listen: first the basses, round; then the nylon trebles, sweet.
l112.s4: "No steel strings on a classical guitar: it isn't built for that tension."
l112.c1b: The 6th, 5th and 4th have wire wrapped around them and sound low and round. The 3rd, 2nd and 1st are plain nylon. Listen to them.
l112.c2b: The classical guitar is built for the low tension of nylon. Steel strings can bend the neck or lift the bridge.
l112.c3b: Keep it in its case, away from the sun and heaters. Wash your hands before playing: the strings last longer.
l112.q1: Which strings are wound (wrapped in wire)?
l112.q2: What strings does a classical guitar use?
l112.play: Play the three open bass strings first, then the three trebles. Hear the difference.

l113.title: The names of the strings
l113.objective: Name each string by number and by note, and find it without looking at the list.
l113.s1: "To play with others we need to speak the same language: the number and the name of each string."
l113.s2: The numbers go from the thinnest to the thickest: 1st E, 2nd B, 3rd G, 4th D, 5th A and 6th E.
l113.s3: Listen to the 5th, A, and the 4th, D. Each one has its own name and sound.
l113.s4: "A trick: E, A, D, G, B, E, from low to high. Say it out loud while you play."
l113.c1b: Look at the drawing: each string has a number (from the 1st, the thinnest, to the 6th, the thickest) and the name of the note it plays open.
l113.c2b: From the 6th to the 1st: E, A, D, G, B and E. Each one higher than the last.
l113.c3b: In scores and in the app you'll see letters: E, A, D, G, B and E. In Spanish and Portuguese they are Mi, La, Re, Sol, Si and Mi.
l113.q1: Which number is the A string?
l113.tap: Tap these open strings on the fretboard: D, B, A and G.
l113.play: Play the open string that lights up: A, G, high E, D, B and low E.

l114.title: Tune with the app
l114.objective: Tune all 6 strings with the app's tuner, within ±5 cents.
l114.s1: "Always tune before you play. Nylon goes out of tune more than steel, especially when it's hot or cold."
l114.s2: Play a string and watch the needle: to the left it's flat; to the right, sharp.
l114.s3: Turn the peg slowly while the string rings, until the needle sits in the teal zone.
l114.s4: "Always tune up to the note: if you go past it, drop a little and come back up."
l114.c1b: The needle shows whether the string is flat (left), sharp (right) or in tune (teal zone, ±5 cents).
l114.c2b: Listen to how they sound in tune: E, A, D, G, B and E.
l114.c3b: The pegs stick out the sides of the slotted headstock. Each turn moves the pitch a lot: turn a little at a time.
l114.ear: Listen to two notes. Is the second one higher or lower?
l114.tune: Tune all 6 strings: play each one until the needle sits in the teal zone.

l115.title: New strings
l115.objective: Know when to change strings, how to tie them, and why you'll need to retune several times.
l115.s1: "My strings sound dull and won't stay in tune. Time to change them!"
l115.s2: On a classical guitar, each string is tied with a knot at the bridge and wound around a roller in the headstock.
l115.s3: New nylon strings stretch: you'll retune a lot during the first few days.
l115.s4: "Change the strings one at a time, so the neck doesn't lose all its tension at once."
l115.c1b: Every 2 or 3 months if you play daily, or sooner if they sound dull, show dents or won't tune up the neck.
l115.c2b: Thread the string through the bridge, tie it back on itself and take it to the headstock. Leave 2 or 3 turns on the roller.
l115.c3b: Nylon keeps stretching for a few days. Tune, play a while and tune again: that's normal.
l115.q1: How often should you change strings if you play every day?
l115.q1o2: Every 2 or 3 months, or when they sound dull
l115.q2: On a classical guitar, how are the strings attached to the bridge?
l115.q2o2: With a metal ball at the end
l115.q2o3: With a knot at the bridge
l115.q3: You just put on new strings. Why do they go out of tune right away?
l115.q3o1: Because nylon stretches during the first days
l115.tune: Retune all 6 strings: the needle has to sit in the teal zone.

l121.title: Sitting posture
l121.objective: Sit with a straight back and the guitar steady, without holding it up with your hands.
l121.s1: "The classical guitar is played sitting down. If the guitar is steady, your hands are free to play."
l121.s2: Left foot on a footstool, guitar on your left leg, back straight.
l121.s3: The neck tilts upward, with the headstock about level with your shoulder.
l121.s4: "No footstool? A stack of books works. There are also supports that rest on your leg."
l121.c1b: Look at the drawing: the guitar rests on both legs, your chest and your right arm, and stays put even if you let go.
l121.c2b: In folk and rock many players rest it on the right leg, without a footstool. That works too: what matters is a straight back and loose shoulders.
l121.c3b: Everything is mirrored: the right foot goes on the footstool and the guitar on the right leg. In Settings you can choose your hand and the app mirrors the drawings.
l121.q1: In classical posture, where does the guitar rest?
l121.q1o2: On the left leg, with that foot on a footstool
l121.q1o3: Hanging from a strap, standing up
l121.q2o1: Tilted upward, with the headstock about shoulder height
l121.play: Sitting in position, play the string that lights up with your thumb.

l122.title: The picking hand: p-i-m-a
l122.objective: Name the fingers p-i-m-a and play the open basses with your thumb at 60 bpm.
l122.s1: "No pick on a classical guitar: you play with your fingers. And each finger has its letter."
